parts.text: These poems are often unexpected, delightful and poignant. They remind commuters of our humanness and offer

small moments of respite. Whether on an empty platform or in a crowded carriage, Londoners and tourists alike can be moved by the rhythms of poetry.

“I love dis great, polluted place,” says Benjamin Zephaniah in The London Breed (2001). “I sing of a world
,” declares Nigerian poet Niyi Osundare with hope in I Sing of Change (1981). In A Bunch of Consolation (2023), Maura Dooley urges us “to love, to speak up, to hold steady”. A melancholic

for her mother’s cooking in Grace Nichols’ Like a Beacon (1984) – one of the first poems to be featured on a poster – beckons your appetite but breaks your heart.

This year Poems on the Underground has celebrated 40 years of bringing poetry to the commuting

. The first poems to be displayed were Up in the Morning Early (1788) by Robert Burns; The Railway Children (1984) by Seamus Heaney; Like a Beacon (1984) by Grace Nichols; Ozymandias (1818) by Percy Bysshe Shelley; and This Is Just To Say (1934) by William Carlos Williams.

The project was the
of the American essayist and novelist Judith Chernaik, who came up with the idea as a young academic when she moved to London in 1972 with her husband and children. The couple

the Barrow poets Gerard Benson and Cicely Herbert and soon became part of their literary circle. The Barrow poets were a group of writers and folk musicians who got their name from selling poems from handbarrows in local markets.

The couple were
to attend play-reading groups, and in one such gathering, the work being explored was Shakespeare’s As You Like It. Chernaik was

by the figure of Orlando, who hangs poems in the trees of the Forest of Arden for his love, Rosalind.

Imagining the London Underground as a real-life contemporary Forest of Arden, she asked her friends what they thought of her idea to hang some poems in the advertising spaces on the tube. Delighted by the

, they encouraged her, and the following morning, a determined Chernaik wrote to London Transport (later TfL).

To her amazement London Transport replied and was interested in her proposal. She
an Arts Council Grant in 1985 and the rest is literary history: four decades of sharing poetry with the public though Poems on the Underground.

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Ancient disputes over mapmaking illuminate debates about how the world is represented.

A public poetry project connects Shakespeare's influence with everyday journeys on the Underground.
